{"id": "7:91/q10", "question": "Who was Kulman, and what is reported about his death?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q10/p1", "position": "Kulman or Kalman was a Midianite king who burned beneath the cloud and was lamented by his sister or daughter.", "reasons": "Al-Bajalī says the Abjad letter names belonged to kings and gives Kulman as ruler in Shuʿayb's time. The elegy says fire beneath the cloud consumed the settlement and that his death broke the mourner's support. Reports vary between sister and daughter, and between Kalmun, Kalman, Kulman and Kilmān. Al-Ālūsī suggests a believing daughter could have survived the general death, but also questions the report's chain; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls the royal identification speculative."}]}
{"id": "7:91/q11", "question": "What conduct did the punishment answer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q11/p1", "position": "The leaders' unbelief, defiance, threats and boast that Shuʿayb's followers would lose brought a fitting reversal.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr recalls their oath, their threats to expel Shuʿayb and his companions, their mockery of his prayer in 11:87 and demand in 26:187; he says they were shaken as they had shaken others and ties the answer to 26:189. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī observes that the people themselves lost the land and possessions they thought secure. Kur'an Yolu calls the elite unbelieving and oppressive and their disappearance deserved. Jishumī calls the quake the answer to grave corruption."}]}
{"id": "7:91/q12", "question": "How does this verse connect the chiefs' boast to the next verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q12/p1", "position": "It reverses their claim that Shuʿayb's followers would lose: the deniers were the ones destroyed and made losers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this verse first leaves the victims implicit, then 7:92 names the deniers and answers the boast of 7:90. He also stresses their sudden loss of land and possessions. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the fāʾ places punishment immediately after the chiefs' warning."}]}
{"id": "7:91/q13", "question": "What earlier punishment narratives illuminate this one?", "turns_on": "The notes compare the wording and fate with Ṣāliḥ's people or the combined calamity of Lot's people.", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q13/p1", "position": "Ṣāliḥ's people are described with the same wording.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr points to their punishment at 7:78; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī points back to its aṣbaḥa explanation. Iṣlāḥī says the phrase is identical and leaves the physical nature unspecified; Study Quran says Midian's destruction matches Thamūd's."}, {"id": "7:91/q13/p2", "position": "Lot's nearby people suffered a comparable combined punishment.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī connects Shuʿayb's warning at Hūd 11:89 with Lot, calls Lot's punishment a stone-hurling wind, and says its ḥāṣib combines rajfah, ṣayḥah and ẓullah; he says both nearby peoples meet the same fate."}]}
{"id": "7:91/q14", "question": "How does this destruction fit the sūra's sequence of messenger stories?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q14/p1", "position": "It concludes the series of rejected messengers and destroyed oppressors in 7:59–92 or 7:93.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī frames 7:59–92 as the continuing promised messenger mission and says Section VI uses Arabian nations' histories to warn Quraysh of judgment after authority, injustice, rejection and respite. He says the nations were known around Arabia and the accounts are historically ordered, beginning with Noah. Kur'an Yolu calls the five prior prophet accounts concise lessons in calls, responses and disasters, not history for its own sake. Study Quran says this narrative recounts destruction after rejection."}]}
{"id": "7:91/q15", "question": "What lesson does the destruction carry for later peoples?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q15/p1", "position": "After a messenger comes, rejecting reform brings destruction; Quraysh should recognize the warning and impending judgment.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī calls this God's law for every nation, says Quraysh knew vague traditions but missed their moral lessons, and sees the histories of once powerful unjust nations as Quraysh's own warning. Kur'an Yolu says calamities and hardships in the ensuing verses aim at reform and that Shuʿayb had done all he could to rescue his people, leaving no reason to pity them. The elite's deserved catastrophe is another example."}]}
{"id": "7:91/q16", "question": "How does the destructive sign compare with signs in Muhammad's time?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q16/p1", "position": "The same sort of frightening angelic force accompanied Muhammad, the prophet of mercy, as a means of salvation.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī compares reports of angels at Ḥunayn, unbelievers hearing a pebble-like sound within themselves, and an enemy feeling terror a month's journey in front and behind; here it destroyed, while with Muhammad it saved."}]}
{"id": "7:91/q17", "question": "What inward meaning is given to their crouching death?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q17/p1", "position": "Their bodily collapse mirrors spirits squatting in bodily abodes after stubbornness made truth look false and success look like loss.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports this as the Najmiyya interpretation."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q01", "question": "Who are those described as denying Shuʿayb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q01/p1", "position": "The unbelieving people of Midian, including the oppressive chiefs who threatened Shuʿayb and his followers.", "reasons": "Elmalılı identifies them with those who threatened expulsion; Kur'an Yolu specifies Midian's unbelieving, oppressive elite and their deserved catastrophe."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q02", "question": "How is the first 'those who denied Shuʿayb' construed?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative begins a fresh assertion or depends syntactically on the later clause or the chiefs' preceding speech; al-Samīn also disputes the precise antecedent of the attached reading.", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q02/p1", "position": "It starts an independent nominal sentence as subject, with the comparison as predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr give the subject–predicate analysis. Abū Ḥayyān rejects attached parses as strained. Al-Jurjānī, as reported by al-Qurṭubī, says the sentence begins anew; al-Wāḥidī also calls the repeated clause a fresh nominal sentence."}, {"id": "7:92/q02/p2", "position": "The second relative clause and its predicate complete the first subject; the comparison is parenthetical or circumstantial to 'denied.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this parse; Abū al-Baqāʾ allows the second clause as predicate and the simile as a circumstance of the pronoun in كذبوا. Al-Ālūsī reports this among Abū al-Baqāʾ's alternatives. Abū Ḥayyān considers such attachment strained."}, {"id": "7:92/q02/p3", "position": "The comparison and the second relative clause are two predicates of the first relative subject.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives the second relative as a second predicate, and allows it as first or second predicate in his survey."}, {"id": "7:92/q02/p4", "position": "The first relative is attached to the earlier chiefs' speech as a modifier or apposition; the comparison is circumstantial.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ allows modification or replacement of قومه. Al-Samīn reports apposition to الذين كفروا من قومه in 7:90, reports an adjective of that phrase from Abū al-Baqāʾ and the Shaykh, but refines its antecedent to الملأ and prefers apposition to, or an adjective of, الملأ. Abū Ḥayyān calls the attached analyses strained."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q03", "question": "What does 'yaghnu fīhā' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ghaniya is taken from residence, or from wealth and sufficiency; some reports paraphrase the resulting image more broadly as never having existed.", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q03/p1", "position": "To dwell, remain, or settle there, often for a long time; the comparison says they seemed never to have inhabited it.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, al-Aṣmaʿī through al-Zajjāj, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite ghaniya bi-makān and maghnā/maghānī ('dwelling[s]'). Al-Ṭabarī cites an anonymous yaghni line and Ruʾba's maghnā; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī cite Labīd and Ḥātim; al-Jishumī cites Muhalhil and Labīd; Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites the line between al-Ḥajūn and al-Ṣafā, neighbors' pact, 'وقد نغنى بها', 'المغانيا', and Muhalhil. Ibn ʿAbbās' reports range from inhabiting to inhabiting for a long time; al-Rāghib adds that long residence makes another place unnecessary. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites Muhalhil and Labīd; her Ibn ʿAbbās report also has an 'never existed' version. Al-Thaʿlabī includes staying and enjoying life in his broad gloss; al-Biqāʿī notes vanished leisure and self-sufficiency."}, {"id": "7:92/q03/p2", "position": "To live there in ease, prosperity, enjoyment, or self-sufficiency.", "reasons": "Qatāda's gloss is widely transmitted, sometimes pairing dwelling with enjoyment. Al-Zajjāj, Ibn al-Anbārī, and al-Samīn connect the sense to wealth or freedom from need, rather than bare residence; al-Zajjāj and al-Ālūsī cite Ḥātim's verse contrasting poverty and wealth, and al-Samīn cites al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur's 'بأنعم عيشة'. Ibn ʿAṭiyya's poetry survey finds residence accompanied by ease, perhaps from istighnāʾ; Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr report it. Al-Jishumī says a home makes its occupant independent of other places. Al-Rāghib likewise joins long residence with sufficiency. Al-Biqāʿī mentions their lost leisure and celebration."}, {"id": "7:92/q03/p3", "position": "It says they seemed never to have been or existed there at all.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd, Abū Mālik, Muqātil and later reports use the broad gloss 'never there'; al-Ṭabrisī and al-Itqān call it never existing, the latter citing Labīd's 'غن

{"id": "7:92/q04", "question": "What does the comparison with never having lived there convey?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either the total removal of people and traces or the contrast between deep rootedness and a transient stay.", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q04/p1", "position": "Their punishment so completely erased them and their traces that their former settled life seemed never to have happened.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says their town was left empty; Ibn ʿAṭiyya stresses complete destruction as a lesson. Al-Bayḍāwī says they were uprooted, and Abū Ḥayyān links the emptied place to 10:24 and a poem about Makkah without its inhabitants. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the point is erasure of traces rather than ordinary death, compares 10:24 and 69:8, and infers earthquake and lightning burned and buried bodies and overturned dwellings. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says the quake left them dead amid homes, kin, estates and possessions they had been deeply rooted in; Kur'an Yolu and The Study Quran also identify the catastrophic erasure."}, {"id": "7:92/q04/p2", "position": "It depicts even an established population as though it had stayed only briefly and could leave its land without difficulty.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ contrasts transient residents with people bound by kin, homes, estates, and possessions; the instant loss of that rooted life drives the simile."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q05", "question": "What is the form of 'kaʾan' here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q05/p1", "position": "It is a lightened form of kaʾanna before a verbal clause.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ attributes the lightening to its introduction of a verbal clause."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q06", "question": "What does fronting the first relative clause convey?", "turns_on": "The notes differ in the effect they draw from making the relative clause the subject: exclusive allocation, causal implication, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q06/p1", "position": "It singles out the deniers for annihilation and implies the escape of Shuʿayb's followers.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf states exclusive destruction; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report this from al-Zamakhsharī. Al-Samīn equates the claim of اختصاص with restriction but notes disagreement over its force in noun-first versus predicate-first formulations. Al-Ālūsī says the earlier contrast of the two groups and the relative subject can yield exclusivity."}, {"id": "7:92/q06/p2", "position": "Making denial the subject hints that denial caused the lasting destruction.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the predicate's dependence on the relative subject signals causation and the believers' lasting escape; Ibn ʿĀshūr also reads the relative wording as punishment for denial."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q07", "question": "How is the repeated 'those who denied Shuʿayb' construed in the second sentence?", "turns_on": "Whether the repetition starts a self-contained sentence, completes the first subject, or is dependent by apposition or an implied verb.", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q07/p1", "position": "It begins a fresh independent nominal sentence, with 'they were the losers' as its predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān parse it this way; al-Samīn calls this the clearest analysis. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bursawī describe the second clause as a new or resumptive address."}, {"id": "7:92/q07/p2", "position": "It is the predicate, or one of two predicates, of the first relative clause.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ and al-Samīn allow this attached analysis, with the comparison circumstantial or as another predicate. Al-Ālūsī also reports it."}, {"id": "7:92/q07/p3", "position": "It apposes the pronoun in 'yaghnaw.'", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ offers this parse, reported by Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī; Abū Ḥayyān prefers an independent subject."}, {"id": "7:92/q07/p4", "position": "It is an accusative specification after an implied 'I mean.'", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ offers the omitted أعني construction, also listed by al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī; Abū Ḥayyān prefers independence."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q08", "question": "Why repeat 'those who denied Shuʿayb' instead of using a pronoun?", "turns_on": "Al-Ālūsī questions whether every rhetorical effect attributed to the single verse follows without taking both resumptions together.", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q08/p1", "position": "The repetition intensifies blame, humiliation, the magnitude of their denial, loss, and deserved punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī compares repeated Arab accusations; al-Rāzī says Arabs repeat for emphasis. Al-Kashshāf says the fresh opening rebuts and mocks the chiefs' advice and magnifies their fate; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī transmit this. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Bayḍāwī note the independent nominal sentences; al-Biqāʿī stresses the shame of losing bodies and souls. Al-Ṭībī says two resumptions answer two questions, first what happened after the quake and then whether ruin reached others; his second clause is emphatic and exclusive. Al-Ālūsī reports a customary Arab unconnected rebuke with the example of a brother who plundered property and violated protection. Al-Ālūsī objects that all of al-Kashshāf's effects are hard to infer from this verse alone, saying the two resumptions together suggest them more clearly."}, {"id": "7:92/q08/p2", "position": "The repetition also warns the Arab polytheist audience through the earlier deniers' fate.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the repeated identification enumerates and awakens them, with the warning made explicit in 47:10."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q09", "question": "Who are 'the losers'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q09/p1", "position": "Shuʿayb's deniers themselves, while his believing followers escaped and gained.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ, Iṣlāḥī, and The Study Quran set the answer against the chiefs' claim in 7:90 that following Shuʿayb would bring loss. Al-Kashshāf, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ṭībī say the second opening restricts great loss to the deniers. Al-Bayḍāwī says the believers gained in both abodes; al-Ālūsī notes their rescue is explicit in 11:94."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q10", "question": "What loss do the deniers suffer?", "turns_on": "Al-Māwardī preserves distinct glosses of loss by unbelief and by destruction; several later sources include both worldly and religious loss.", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q10/p1", "position": "Loss through unbelief, or loss of religion and the next life.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports unbelief as one explanation. The Study Quran calls them deluded about true religion."}, {"id": "7:92/q10/p2", "position": "Loss through destruction and loss of worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī attributes the destruction gloss to Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī say they lost both worldly and religious life; al-Biqāʿī specifies bodies and souls. Al-Ṭībī says the definite generic 'losers' magnifies the loss."}, {"id": "7:92/q10/p3", "position": "Khusr is the loss of one's capital.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives the lexical sense and notes the related verb for incurring loss."}]}

{"id": "7:92/q13", "question": "How does the verse answer the chiefs' earlier threats and warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q13/p1", "position": "The deniers, who threatened to expel Shuʿayb and the believers, were themselves driven out permanently by destruction.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī connect this to 7:88; Ibn Kathīr locates the punishment in the homes from which they had planned expulsion. {"id": "7:92/q15", "question": "What does the selective punishment show?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q15/p1", "position": "Its cause is a freely acting creator, rather than stars or nature, which would have struck followers too.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues from the fact that only the deniers were punished in the same town."}, {"id": "7:92/q15/p2", "position": "Its cause knows particulars and distinguishes obedient from disobedient people.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues that the selective destruction requires knowledge of each person's state."}, {"id": "7:92/q15/p3", "position": "It is a great miracle establishing Shuʿayb's truth.", "reasons": "For al-Rāzī, the survival of some alongside the punishment of others in the town proves the messenger's claim."}]}
{"id": "7:92/q16", "question": "What wider lesson is drawn from the deniers' fate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:92/q16/p1", "position": "Deniers may prevail briefly, but their traces vanish while truth's followers ultimately prevail.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī states this lesson and reports Masnavi verses recalling the deniers publicly and urging alliance with the victorious side."}, {"id": "7:92/q16/p2", "position": "Once Shuʿayb had exhausted efforts to rescue them from error, there was no reason to pity their fate.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu ties this judgment to his work to avert their catastrophe."}, {"id": "7:92/q16/p3", "position": "The same law of response to a messenger applies to nations: accept reform or face destruction.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the nations were granted political authority, became ungrateful and unjust, rejected messengers and were destroyed after respite; the accounts warn Quraysh of the same judgment."}, {"id": "7:92/q16/p4", "position": "These prophetic accounts teach the moral of calls, responses, and disasters; subsequent hardship aims at reform.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu describes the five preceding accounts as concise lessons rather than history for its own sake and says the ensuing calamities and hardships seek reform."}]}

{"id": "7:150/q01", "question": "When did Moses learn of the calf worship?", "turns_on": "Whether 7:150 describes anger before arrival and whether 20:85 supplies prior notice.", "positions": [{"id": "7:150/q01/p1", "position": "God had informed Moses at the mountain before his return; Ṭā Hā 20:85 supports this.", "reasons": "MUQATIL (author): Moses returned angry and sorrowful over calf worship, already informed by God on the Mount. TAB-FULL (author): Moses returned angry and grieved after God told him the Samaritan had led his tested people astray. IBNABIHATIM (author): Prophet: God informed Moses but he cast tablets only after seeing idolatry. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الطبري): Al-Tabari says God informed Moses before his return that the Israelites had been led astray by the calf, so Moses returned angry. RAZI-FULL (أبو مسلم): Abu Muslim says Moses already knew beforehand; al-Razi prefers this because the verse says he was angry while returning, before reaching them, and Ta Ha says God told him at the appointed meeting. | mentions 20:85 RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi’s first argument for prior knowledge is that Moses was already angry and grieving while still on his way, before reaching the people. RAZI-FULL (author): His second argument is that Ta Ha says God informed Moses of the event at the appointed meeting. | mentions 20:85 QURTUBI-FULL (الطبري): Al-Ṭabarī says God had told Moses before he returned that the people had been tested by the calf, so Moses came back angry. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الطبري): Al-Tabari says God informed Moses before he returned that his people had been seduced by the calf, explaining his anger; the author links this to the verse in Ta-Ha. | mentions 20:85 IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن عباس عن النبي): The Prophet says Moses did not throw the tablets when God informed him that his people had fallen into trial; seeing them himself moved him to throw them, for seeing is unlike hearing. BIQAI-FULL (author): Moses returned from intimate communion angry and sorrowful because God had informed him that his people worshipped the calf; his anger was for God. DURR-FULL (النبي): The Prophet says seeing is unlike hearing: God told Moses his people had been led astray, but when Moses saw them he cast the tablets and some broke. BURSEVI (author): Moses returned from Mount Sinai intensely angry; the word asaf means anger, as in “when they angered Us.” God had informed him during the conversation that his people worshipped the calf. | mentions 43:55 ALUSI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas reports from the Prophet that God had told Moses his people were tested, but Moses did not cast the tablets until he saw them; some then broke. TABATABAI (author): Moses returned angry after God told him that his people had gone astray; he reproached them for badly succeeding him and hastening their Lord's affair.
